meta.title: Czech B2
meta.subtitle: 1,200 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Czech → English (see the Czech, recall the meaning) and English → Czech (see an English meaning, recall the Czech). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1,200 words and expressions for level B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no Czech exam board publishes a word list beyond A2 — the A1 and A2 decks follow the official list of the permanent-residence exam, but the B1 citizenship exam and Charles University's CCE exams publish none. So 263 of the 1,200 words were written for Folio, a topic at a time, for the themes of the Council of Europe's B2 specification, Vantage (van Ek and Trim, 2001), which carries the Threshold Level's themes a level further: work and careers, the economy and money, the state, politics and society, law and crime, the media and technology, science and research, health care, the environment, culture and the arts, education and relationships — the next layer of vocabulary beyond A1 to B1 — together with the words of opinion and argument the level needs. They are Folio's choice, not an exam board's, and this is not an official word list. The other 937 are the commonest words of everyday Czech not already chosen, from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles, each word counted over all its forms. No word taught in A1, A2 or B1 is repeated. The cards are ordered by that frequency, so the words met most often come first; the 4 multi-word expressions, which a list of single words cannot count, come last. Czech changes the endings of its nouns, adjectives and verbs, and stems change with them, so each card carries the forms that cannot be guessed, read from a dictionary rather than generated. 626 nouns show their gender, three cases of the singular and two of the plural. 288 verbs show their aspect and its partner, the forms for já (I), on (he) and oni (they) and the past of on — a perfective verb's present forms being its future. 23 adjectives show their comparative and superlative. Real example sentences come with 1,026 of the 1,200 words, three apiece for 728, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Meanings, forms and parts of speech: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency ordering: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
